stockRace.noLock.title: Without FOR UPDATE
stockRace.noLock.introduction: Three units of SKU-C sit in one bin. Orders A and B each want all three and arrive at the same moment. In this version the bin row is read without a lock.
stockRace.noLock.step1: A opens a transaction and reads the bin. Nothing is reserved, so all three units look available.
stockRace.noLock.step2: B does the same a moment later. A has written nothing yet, so B sees exactly what A saw: three units available.
stockRace.noLock.step3: A reserves its three units. The new value, 0 + 3, was computed in the application from what A read. Postgres takes the row lock for this write and keeps it until A commits.
stockRace.noLock.step4: B writes its own 0 + 3. Postgres makes B wait for A's row lock, so the two writes cannot interleave — but the number B is about to write was decided on a read that is already out of date.
stockRace.noLock.step5: A commits and releases the lock. B's write goes through at once and replaces A's 3 with B's 3. A's reservation has disappeared from the count, and nobody was told.
stockRace.noLock.step6: B commits. Both orders were told they hold three units: six units promised, three on the shelf.
stockRace.noLock.outcome: A lost update. The row says three are reserved, each order believes it holds three, and three units are oversold. There was no error and no constraint violation: every write stored a legal value.
stockRace.withLock.title: With FOR UPDATE
stockRace.withLock.introduction: The same shelf and the same two orders. This time the bins are read with SELECT … FOR UPDATE, which is what warehouse does.
stockRace.withLock.step1: A opens a transaction and reads the bin with FOR UPDATE. The row lock is taken at the read, so nothing can change the row between A's decision and A's write.
stockRace.withLock.step2: B asks for the same row FOR UPDATE and waits. It has not read anything yet, so it has nothing stale to act on. Warehouse bounds this wait with a lock_timeout that applies to this transaction only.
stockRace.withLock.step3: A reserves its three units, computed from the value it read under the lock.
stockRace.withLock.step4: A commits and the lock passes to B. B's read completes now and returns the row as A left it: three reserved, none available.
stockRace.withLock.step5: No bin can cover three units, so warehouse refuses with INSUFFICIENT_STOCK and rolls B's transaction back, taking B's ledger rows with it.
stockRace.withLock.outcome: Three units on the shelf, three promised. B was refused on the true count instead of being given stock that no longer existed.

stack.planned.android.summary: Customer app for Android, written natively.
stack.planned.ios.summary: Customer app for iOS, written natively.
stack.planned.backoffice.summary: One operator console for every service, built on the APIs each service owns.
stack.docs.summary: This documentation: static pages, interactive diagrams as islands, two languages.
stack.planned.recommendation.summary: Product recommendations, as its own service with its own data.
stack.edge.gateway.summary: The only entry point from the internet: routing, CORS and rate limits, declared in Pkl and run without a database.
stack.edge.contracts.summary: The single definition of every message on the wire, published as a package for each language that consumes it.
stack.edge.courier.summary: The courier app: assigned deliveries, proof of delivery and live location, through the gateway.
stack.platform.data.summary: PostgreSQL for each service's own database, Redis for the order service's carts, Typesense for the search index.
stack.platform.trust.summary: Services prove who they are to each other with certificates carrying SPIFFE IDs, issued by step-ca. Secrets are encrypted at rest with SOPS and age.
stack.platform.observability.summary: Metrics in Prometheus, logs shipped by Promtail into Loki, dashboards and alerting in Grafana.
stack.delivery.containers.summary: Every service ships as a container image, and environments are described with Docker Compose.
stack.delivery.pipelines.summary: Repositories build, test and scan themselves on GitHub Actions, with GitLab CI on the mirror.
stack.delivery.infrastructure.summary: Servers are declared with OpenTofu, and part of the operational tooling is written in D.

saga.label.empty: No rows yet: nothing has been attempted.
saga.succeeds.title: Everything answers
saga.succeeds.introduction: A cart of two products from one merchant, with a voucher and one item on a flash sale. Before any of this, order priced the cart with pricing, wrote the order as PENDING_PAYMENT and opened a saga. Every step below is written to the saga log as Attempting before its call goes out.
saga.succeeds.step1: Redeem the voucher. pricing records a redemption row for this order — the ledger entry that makes it possible to give the voucher back later.
saga.succeeds.step2: Claim the flash-sale unit before touching the shelf. It is the scarcer resource; failing on it after reserving stock would mean undoing more.
saga.succeeds.step3: Reserve the first product in warehouse, under the row lock from the first lesson.
saga.succeeds.step4: One row per product: the second reservation is its own step, so each can be released on its own.
saga.succeeds.step5: Hold the money in escrow. payment moves it from the customer's wallet into a hold, keyed by the order number so a repeat cannot take it twice.
saga.succeeds.step6: Only now is warehouse told there is an order to pick. A fulfilment task created earlier could be picked for an order that is about to be unwound.
saga.succeeds.step7: Every hold is real, so the saga is Completed, the order becomes PAID — and only then is the cart emptied.
saga.succeeds.outcome: Six calls, six rows Done, one answer to the customer: 201 Created.
saga.refused.title: Warehouse refuses
saga.refused.introduction: The same checkout, but the shelf holds only one unit of SKU-B and the cart wants two.
saga.refused.step4: warehouse refuses SKU-B with INSUFFICIENT_STOCK, inside the same transaction that would have taken the units. Nothing is held for this row, so it is recorded Failed and will not be compensated.
saga.refused.step5: Compensation starts from the newest row and works backwards. SKU-A goes back to the shelf first.
saga.refused.step6: Then the flash-sale unit goes back to the sale.
saga.refused.step7: Then the voucher redemption is released, so the customer can use the voucher again.
saga.refused.step8: Everything is given back: the saga is Compensated and the order is kept as CANCELLED, not deleted. The customer gets 409 CHECKOUT_ROLLED_BACK with the order number and warehouse's reason.
saga.refused.outcome: Nothing is held anywhere, and the order explains itself: a cancelled checkout with a reason, not one that silently never happened.
saga.silent.title: Payment does not answer
saga.silent.introduction: The voucher and the stock are held, then the call to payment runs out of time. order cannot tell whether the hold was created before the connection gave up.
saga.silent.step3: CreateEscrowHold is written as Attempting, sent, and never answered. The row stays Attempting: order does not know whether money moved. The checkout gives up — "a service this checkout depends on did not answer" — and starts compensating.
saga.silent.step4: An Attempting row is compensated exactly like a Done one: undoing too much is safe, undoing too little strands money. The refund goes out under the same order-keyed idempotency key, and had its answer been unclear, order would read payment's ledger with GetEscrowStatus before deciding.
saga.silent.step5: SKU-A goes back to the shelf.
saga.silent.step7: The saga is Compensated and the customer gets 409 CHECKOUT_ROLLED_BACK. Whether or not the first hold had landed, nothing is held now.
saga.silent.outcome: A call with no answer is treated as possibly done. pricing and warehouse answer a release for something never taken as a success; for money, order goes further and confirms against payment's ledger before closing the row.
saga.stuck.title: A release fails
saga.stuck.introduction: warehouse refuses SKU-B again, but this time pricing is down while the saga unwinds.
saga.stuck.step3: warehouse refuses SKU-B: Failed, nothing held.
saga.stuck.step5: Releasing the voucher fails with UNAVAILABLE. A transient error neither stops the round nor counts as success: the voucher row stays Done, still held. The saga ends Stuck with its next round due in 15–30 s — and the customer already has their 409.
saga.stuck.step6: StuckSagaSweeper runs every minute and takes over due sagas under a fresh lease. The retry re-sends only what is still held: the voucher, not SKU-A.
saga.stuck.step7: The voucher comes back and the saga is Compensated. Had pricing stayed down, the delay would keep doubling up to 30 minutes, and after the sixth round the saga is Abandoned and logged GIVING UP for a person to settle.
saga.stuck.outcome: A partial unwind is never reported as a complete one. Stuck means still holding something and retrying; Abandoned means a person must look.
trust.verdict.asserted: states a fact it does not own
trust.price.title: The unit price
trust.price.introduction: Adding a product to the cart and checking out — as it worked until order v0.1.11, and as it works now.
trust.price.step1: Before: the request to add a product carried its own UnitPrice, and its title, category and merchant too. The cart stored every field exactly as sent.
trust.price.step2: At checkout, order built the price lines from the cart's numbers. pricing applied flash sales and discounts correctly — to the base price it was handed, which the buyer had written.
trust.price.step3: The escrow hold debited that figure, and the merchant would have been paid it. Any signed-in buyer could set the price of anything, and nothing failed: every service did its own job correctly.
trust.price.step4: After: the request carries only what the buyer actually decides — which product, and how many.
trust.price.step5: order asks catalog, the owner of products, for the price, title and merchant, and refreshes a line already in the cart instead of keeping the figure it was added with.
trust.price.step6: Checkout asks catalog again and prices from its answer, not from the cart. That second lookup protected carts saved before the fix, which live in Redis for fourteen days.
trust.price.outcome: The price is the one catalog holds. Fixed in order v0.1.11, and in production since 24 September 2026.
trust.shipping.title: The shipping fee
trust.shipping.introduction: Checking out with a shipping tier — as checkout worked before September 2026, and as it works now.
trust.shipping.step1: Before: the checkout request carried BaseShippingFee and DistanceKm, both defaulting to 0. A buyer who sent nothing had still sent a fee.
trust.shipping.step2: order passed the buyer's fee to pricing as the base shipping fee. pricing applied its shipping discounts on top of whatever arrived; it had no way to know the base was forged.
trust.shipping.step3: The escrow hold took the result: free shipping for anyone who asked for it.
trust.shipping.step4: After: the request names a tier — a choice — and no amount. A fee posted anyway is ignored.
trust.shipping.step5: order asks matching which courier tiers can serve the delivery, and pricing what each tier costs from its rate card. A tier that is not offered is refused rather than priced.
trust.shipping.step6: pricing's final shipping fee must be a discount of its own quote. If it is negative or above the quote, the checkout is refused before an order row exists.
trust.shipping.outcome: The fee comes from the services that own couriers and rates. A request can choose a tier; it cannot name a price.
trust.topUp.title: The wallet top-up
trust.topUp.introduction: Topping up a wallet — as it worked until 14 September 2026, and as it works now.
trust.topUp.step1: Before: a top-up request carried an amount of at least IDR 1,000, with no upper limit. The payment method was accepted and never used.
trust.topUp.step2: payment credited the wallet with that amount straight away. No charge was made, so nothing was paid.
trust.topUp.step3: The balance could then be spent through checkout escrow. Money was created by asking for it.
trust.topUp.step4: After: the amount is still the customer's choice, but only as the amount to be charged. payment records the top-up as PENDING under its Idempotency-Key, asks Midtrans to charge it, and answers 202 with payment instructions.
trust.topUp.step5: When Midtrans reports the payment, payment first verifies the notification's SHA-512 signature, then sets its contents aside and asks Midtrans's status API itself what happened to this order.
trust.topUp.step6: Only a settled payment whose amount equals the recorded one is credited — once, under a lock on the wallet's owner. Anything else credits nothing.
trust.topUp.outcome: The customer chooses how much to pay, the payment provider says what was paid, and only then does money appear. Fixed on 14 September 2026, before production launched.
